                  <!-- # Comparison to a Non-Parametric Quantile Model -->
                  
                  <!-- ```md -->
                  <!-- [draft for promotion — MCF to review] -->
                  
                  <!-- To check that the accumulator model is not imposing its shape on the data, we compare -->
                  <!-- its model-implied quantile fan to a *non-parametric* benchmark: a GAMLSS beta-regression -->
                  <!-- of proportion-produced on age (a penalized spline on the mean and on the scale; the model -->
                                                        <!-- used for the CDI norms), fit to the same per-administration sumscores. Across all five -->
                  <!-- datasets the parametric fan (@fig-gamlss-overlay, blue) tracks both the non-parametric -->
                  <!-- GAMLSS fit (orange) and the empirical quantiles (circles) — the accelerating accumulator -->
                  <!-- is a faithful, low-dimensional compression of the data's quantile structure, not an -->
<!-- artifact of its functional form. -->

<!-- Two implementation notes. First, we let the GAMLSS choose its smoothing by marginal -->
<!-- likelihood; over-smoothing the mean spline makes the non-parametric fit artificially -->
<!-- tight at older ages. Second, we draw each simulated child's curve from the model's -->
<!-- *fitted* per-child acceleration $\kappa_i$ rather than a fresh Gaussian resample of the -->
<!-- population variance. This matters because the fitted acceleration distribution is -->
<!-- right-skewed with a light lower tail (@fig-kappa-skew): a symmetric resample invents -->
<!-- low-acceleration children who do not exist and over-disperses the lower tail at older -->
<!-- ages, whereas the fitted-$\kappa$ fan matches the empirical quantiles at every age. -->
<!-- ``` -->
